title: The French Advance
standfirst: The French Defence hands Black a solid position and one long-term problem. The Advance Variation takes space and makes that problem permanent — read this one alongside the Caro-Kann study.

steps.title: One structure, two openings
body: The French and the Caro-Kann reach almost the same pawn structure by different routes. The difference is one bishop, and it decides how both games are played.
Play this study, then play the Caro-Kann Advance. The contrast is the lesson.

steps.title: Solid, and slightly self-blocking
body: Black prepares …d5 with support. It's tough and reliable — but notice which piece the e6 pawn has just shut in: the light-squared bishop on c8. Keep watching it.

steps.title: Take the whole thing
body: White happily builds the ideal centre while Black prepares.

steps.title: The confrontation
body: Now White must decide: trade, defend, or push.

steps.title: Advance — grab space and close the door
body: The pawn goes past rather than trading. The centre locks, White owns more space, and the c8 bishop is now sealed behind its own pawns with no way out.
Locked centre means play happens on the wings. White will play for a kingside attack; Black must counter on the queenside.

steps.title: Attack the base of the chain
body: The standard rule for a locked pawn chain: attack it at the base. White's chain is d4–e5, so d4 is the target and …c5 is how Black hits it. This move is almost automatic in the French.

steps.title: Prop up the base
body: The obvious answer — hold d4 with a pawn rather than a piece, keeping the chain intact.

steps.title: Another attacker on d4
body: Black keeps piling up on the one square that matters.

steps.title: Another defender
body: White develops and defends in the same move. The little battle over d4 is the whole opening.

steps.title: The queen joins the pile
body: A third attacker on d4, and awkward to meet: the natural developing move Bd3 no longer defends it. The French player's queen almost always ends up here.

steps.title: The modest square, on purpose
body: Not the aggressive d3, because that square is now unavailable — the bishop keeps d4 defended by staying humble. Understanding why beats memorising where.

steps.title: The battle lines are drawn
body: The structure is set. White will castle, hold d4, and build toward a kingside attack with the extra space; Black will keep hammering the queenside.
And that bishop on c8 is still looking at its own pawn on e6. In the Caro-Kann study, watch what Black does differently on move two.
